titre: Henry Dunant, Founder of the Red Cross, Who Died in a Hospice
accroche: In 1859, a horrified witness of the Battle of Solferino invents the Red Cross. Ruined eight years later, he ends up forgotten in a Swiss hospice.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the evening of June 24, 1859, a Swiss businessman passing through, Henry Dunant, arrives at Solferino, in northern Italy, a few hours after one of the deadliest battles of the century. Nearly 40,000 French, Piedmontese, and Austrian soldiers lie dead, dying, or wounded on the battlefield, with almost no medical service to help them. Dunant urgently organizes relief with the inhabitants of the neighboring village of Castiglione, without regard to nationality: a gesture that was far from obvious at the time, in the middle of a war.

## From Testimony to Institution

Back in Geneva, in 1862 Dunant publishes, at his own expense and in 1,600 copies, *Un souvenir de Solférino* (A Memory of Solferino). In it he describes what he saw and proposes two ideas: to create in each country volunteer relief societies formed in peacetime, and to have an international agreement adopted protecting wounded soldiers, whichever side they are on. The idea catches on. On February 17, 1863, a committee of five members meets in Geneva (Dunant, General Guillaume-Henri Dufour, the jurist Gustave Moynier, and the physicians Louis Appia and Théodore Maunoir) and becomes the future International Committee of the Red Cross. The following year, on August 22, 1864, twelve states sign in Geneva the first international convention protecting the wounded and medical personnel in wartime.

## Ruin, Then Oblivion

Dunant does not enjoy this success for long. Involved in financial ventures in Algeria, he is caught up in the collapse of a Geneva bank in 1867. The city's Calvinist bourgeoisie, which already reproaches him for a temperament too generous for business, expels him from the committee he founded: he resigns on August 25, 1867, is struck from its rolls on September 8, and a court convicts him of unfair practices the following year. He leaves Geneva and never returns, wandering for nearly 20 years between Paris, Stuttgart, and Rome, before settling in 1887 in a hospice in the Swiss village of Heiden.

It is there, by chance, that a journalist from St. Gallen, Georg Baumberger, runs into him on a walk in 1895 and discovers that he is talking to the founder of the Red Cross, long believed dead. The article he publishes travels around Europe and restores Dunant's reputation: in time for him to receive, in 1901, the very first Nobel Peace Prize, shared with the French pacifist Frédéric Passy. Dunant would never spend a cent of the award: he has it placed in a Norwegian bank, out of reach of his former creditors, and bequeaths it in his will to charitable causes. He dies on October 30, 1910, still in the hospice at Heiden, with no ceremony other than a discreet burial in a Zurich cemetery.

repere.texte: The 1901 Nobel Peace Prize, the very first awarded, pays Dunant 104,000 Swiss francs. He will never touch them himself: his doctor places them in a Norwegian bank, out of reach of his Geneva creditors, and Dunant bequeaths them in his will to charitable causes.

carte.punch: The founder of the Red Cross, ruined and believed dead, is found by chance in a hospice.
carte.idee: In 1859, Henry Dunant witnesses the horror of Solferino and draws from it the idea of the Red Cross and the first Geneva Convention. Ruined and expelled from the committee in 1867, he ends up in 1887 in a Swiss hospice, where a journalist finds him in 1895, in time for the first Nobel Peace Prize, in 1901.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The page on the 1862 book that gave birth to the Red Cross movement.

quiz.question: Why does Henry Dunant, founder of the Red Cross, become famous again in 1895, after decades of oblivion?
choix: Because he published a second book on the Battle of Solferino
Because he won a lawsuit against his former Geneva creditors
Because a journalist recognized him by chance and published his story
Because the Swiss government officially rehabilitated him
quiz.explication: Georg Baumberger, editor-in-chief of a St. Gallen newspaper, runs into Dunant by chance in Heiden in 1895 and publishes his story; the article, picked up across Europe, gets him rediscovered, then rewarded with the first Nobel Peace Prize six years later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Henry Dunant leave the International Committee he founded, in 1867?
choix: He is caught up in the collapse of a Geneva bank and expelled by the committee
He leaves to head a humanitarian mission in Algeria
He resigns to protest the Franco-Prussian War
He is appointed Swiss ambassador and must leave Geneva
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Involved in financial ventures in Algeria, Dunant is caught up in the collapse of a Geneva bank in 1867, and the city's Calvinist bourgeoisie then expels him from the committee.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to the Nobel Peace Prize money that Dunant receives in 1901?
choix: He spends it to relaunch his former business in Geneva
He places it in a Norwegian bank, out of his creditors' reach
He turns all of it over to the International Committee of the Red Cross
He loses it in a new financial venture in Algeria
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Dunant never spends the sum: his doctor places it in a Norwegian bank, out of reach of his Geneva creditors, before he bequeaths it to charitable causes.
